strengths: Jointly optimizing pipeline placement and per-layer DP, TP, and FSDP choices addresses a useful training-systems problem, with direct relevance to large vision transformers. The proposed integration of profiling, cost modeling, and mathematical optimization is a worthwhile design contribution.

Table 1 shows meaningful practical gains. On EnvB, ViT-Huge reaches 45.58 samples/s versus 38.74 for the strongest baseline, and Swin-Huge reaches 19.08 versus 13.90. UniAP also consistently reduces reported planning time relative to Galvatron, including cases where training throughput ties.

The evaluation spans five hardware environments and includes a 32-device experiment matching exhaustively tuned Megatron throughput. The reported mean estimation error of 3.59%, compared with Galvatron's 11.17%, is encouraging. Algorithm 1, the hardware and solver configurations, and the BERT strategy visualization help explain the approach.
weaknesses: The printed formulation does not enforce valid pipeline ordering. For a two-layer chain u→v, assigning u to stage 2 and v to stage 1 satisfies the contiguity and placement constraints, yet Equation (4) assigns zero communication cost to their edge. Appendix B proves contiguity, which does not establish the required ordering of stage indices. Consequently, the stated optimization can underestimate communication and favor assignments inconsistent with its pipeline model. This is a material concern about the central formulation.

The optimality and complexity claims exceed the evidence. Appendix E specifies a 60-second solver limit and early termination at a relative optimality gap below 4%, but achieved gaps and termination statuses are not reported. Treating a solver timeout as constant in Section 3.5 bounds allotted runtime; it does not establish polynomial-time optimal optimization. Even a completed exact solve would optimize an approximate cost model within the enumerated strategy space.

Memory feasibility is insufficiently explained and validated. Algorithm 1 constructs the memory matrix using micro-batch size b=B/c, but Equation (5) does not show how it accounts for activations retained across c micro-batches under GPipe, especially with activation checkpointing disabled. No peak-memory validation resolves this ambiguity. The throughput estimation error measured only on selected plans also does not establish accurate ranking across candidate strategies.

The ablation does not isolate the central benefit of joint versus hierarchical optimization. Table 2 removes entire categories of parallelism, whereas the principal baselines already combine inter- and intra-layer strategies. Both vision models actually match the inter-layer-only ablation. A comparison using the same candidate space, cost model, and computational budget is missing; hierarchical optimization is not inherently suboptimal merely because it is hierarchical.

Important implementation and measurement details remain incomplete. Equations (3)–(4) contain products of four binary variables, but the auxiliary-variable reformulation needed for the claimed quadratic program is not provided. The checklist states that the full system implementation is withheld. Planning times exclude initial profiling, and differing CPU parallelism complicates attribution of the speedups to the optimization method itself. The undefined meaning of the reported ± values is a smaller presentation issue. Together, the formulation and validation concerns outweigh the demonstrated practical merits in the submitted manuscript.
